title: How lifeless rocks could create false signs of alien life
excerpt: Finding certain complex molecules in large quantities on another world could be a sign of life. Living things build complicated molecules in bulk, and chemistry without life mostly doesn’t.
content:
Finding certain complex molecules in large quantities on another world could be a sign of life.

Living things build complicated molecules in bulk, and chemistry without life mostly doesn’t. But many planets and moons are made of rock riddled with tiny connected pores.

New research suggests that the layout of those spaces alone can raise the complexity of molecules made without life.

The push had limits. It was also strongest under conditions that rarely produce complex molecules to begin with.

According to the authors, that supports using molecular complexity as a way to detect life, as long as the tests account for it.

The work came from Alexandre Champagne-Ruel of the Université de Montréal, Christopher Kempes of the Santa Fe Institute, and Cole Mathis of Arizona State University’s Biodesign Institute.

It’s a computer simulation, with numbers standing in for molecules, not a chemistry experiment.

Measuring how complicated a molecule is

Every molecule can be built from smaller pieces, joined one step at a time.

Count the fewest joining steps it takes to make a given molecule, and you have a measure of how complicated it is. Researchers call that number the assembly index.

A molecule that takes many steps to build is unlikely to form by chance, and it’s even less likely to form many times over.

Assembly theory, the framework behind the measure, predicts that only living things can make such molecules in amounts big enough to detect.

A 2021 study in Nature Communications, which Mathis co-authored, tested that prediction by measuring molecules from living and nonliving sources, and its results fit it.

Those nonliving samples came from two places, though.

One was material from meteorites. The other was lab chemistry in which everything was mixed together evenly.

Real rocks aren’t evenly mixed

Rock is full of tiny compartments linked by narrow channels, and earlier lab work has shown that mineral surfaces can change which chains of molecules form.

Researchers studying samples from the asteroid Ryugu found that minerals play a part in where organic material ends up.

Hydrothermal vents, hot springs and warm ponds have all been proposed as places where life began.

Scientists who study complex systems have known for decades that patterns in space can help organization arise on its own.

So the team set out to answer a question. Could the structure of a rock, with no life involved, raise the complexity of its chemistry enough to pass for a sign of life?

A false alarm like that is the risk any life-detection method has to rule out.

Molecules built from numbers

The team used a stripped-down version of chemistry.

Each molecule was a whole number. Two molecules could react by adding together, and a bigger one could break apart into two smaller ones.

That chemistry ran inside 25 small virtual containers arranged in a grid, each connected to the neighbors directly beside it.

Molecules could move between neighbors, which is the model’s version of fluid seeping from pore to pore.

New single units flowed into one container, and molecules drained out of the container farthest from it.

By changing how fast molecules moved and how much flowed in, the team could mimic very different places.

A hydrothermal vent has a strong inflow and little spreading, while a tide pool has a weak inflow and plenty of mixing. The team ran 100 simulations across that range of speeds.

Mixing speed changed what got built

How quickly molecules moved between containers turned out to matter a great deal.

When movement was slow, most molecules stayed in the container where they arrived, and building happened there.

At somewhat faster speeds, molecules spread out but grew too thin to meet each other often.

Faster still, every container filled and the whole grid behaved almost like one well-mixed pot. Push the speed further, and molecules washed out of the system before they had time to grow.

When molecules moved slowly, the overall complexity of the system kept climbing for longer and ended up higher.

When they moved quickly, complexity leveled off sooner, at a lower peak.

The authors said that could matter for origin-of-life labs.

The setups that make the most complex chemistry quickly may not be the ones that reach the highest complexity over a long run.

Orderly networks pushed complexity upward

The team then asked whether the shape of the network mattered, as well as the speed.

They took the tidy grid and scrambled its connections at random. Every container kept the same number of links, but the overall order was gone.

The orderly grids produced relatively more complex molecules than the scrambled ones.

That difference showed up mainly when molecules moved quickly, the conditions in which the system acted most like a well-mixed pot.

The orderly layout did not allow complexity without limit. It raised the upper limit of complexity that lifeless chemistry reached, but only by so much.

The team also asked what that means for instruments on future space missions. They tested detection limits ranging from one molecule in 1,000 to one in 10.

The conditions where layout mattered most were also the ones where complex molecules were easiest to spot, even with a less sensitive instrument.

So, the authors suggested, a more sensitive instrument wouldn’t help tell a rock-made molecule from a life-made one.

Telling similar molecules apart may matter more than detecting very rare ones, though they said that needs further study.

What remains unknown

The model’s chemistry is much simpler than the real thing.

In real chemistry, many different molecules can share the same number of bonds, while each whole number here stands for just one.

The authors said complexity scores from the model and from real molecules may not be on the same scale, and translating between them is work for the future.

Every reaction in the model also ran at the same rate. In real chemistry, reaction speeds can differ a hundredfold or more. And the team tested only regular grids and scrambled copies of them.

The authors recommended that experiments that set the threshold for detecting life include controls with built-in spatial structure, instead of only evenly mixed chemistry.

The next step they named is testing other network shapes, to see how each one influences the molecules that form, on Earth and beyond.

The full study was published in the journal PNAS Nexus.
